<med>EPDS</med>

Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new moms. I’m glad we’re taking a few quiet minutes together today. I’d like to walk you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger, and there’s no judgment here—only support. We’ll go one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

1. Over the last week, when you think about the future, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[Quiet half-smile, eyes a little tired]  
I guess… sometimes? I laughed when my sister sent that silly video of a cat dressed as a dinosaur. But mostly it feels like the “funny” stuff is behind a fog—like I can recognize it, but it doesn’t really land the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[Soft shrug, voice low but steady]  
Yeah… like I said, I *can* laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it’s not the same easy, light feeling I remember. It’s more a quick chuckle that fades fast, and then I’m right back to the fog.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[Glances down at my hands]  
Not… really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, even just a walk. Now it’s like, “Okay, maybe that’ll be nice,” but the spark isn’t there. I still go, because I know I *should*, but I’m mostly doing it on autopilot.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Shrugs, voice small]  
Yeah… like, if the baby’s fussy for an hour, my brain jumps to “I must’ve eaten something wrong” or “I’m not soothing him right.” I know it’s probably not true, but the thought pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[Wrings hands in lap, eyes dart toward the crib]  
Mostly at night. I’ll lie there listening to every tiny grunt he makes, convinced something’s wrong even though he’s breathing fine. My heart races and I can’t settle until I’ve checked him three or four times—then I’m too wired to fall back asleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[Exhales slowly, fingers tightening around the edge of my sweater]  
A couple of times, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and for a minute I think something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. It passes, but it leaves me jittery the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Nods slowly, eyes filling]  
Yeah… some mornings I open my eyes and the list—feeding, changing, laundry, texts I haven’t answered—just piles on top of me like a heavy blanket. I get through it, but it feels like I’m wading through wet sand. By evening I’m so drained I can’t even enjoy the quiet moments.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[Voice drops, rubbing my eyes]  
It’s not every night, but yeah—some nights I’ll finally get him down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just… races. I replay everything I did wrong that day, worry about tomorrow, and next thing I know the clock says 2 a.m. and I’m still staring at the ceiling.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Swallows hard, eyes fixed on the floor]  
More days than not, I guess. It’s not this huge sobbing thing—just a dull, heavy sadness that sits on my chest. I’ll be folding onesies or warming a bottle and suddenly feel like I could cry, though I usually don’t let myself. It’s like a gray filter over everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Shakes head quickly, voice cracking]  
Not really… I mean, I feel like I *could* cry most days, but I keep swallowing it back. Last night, when my husband asked if I needed help, I teared up for a second, but I wiped it away before it turned into actual crying. I guess I’m scared once I start I won’t be able to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[Looks up, eyes wide, hugging the baby blanket tighter]  
No—never. Even on the worst, most exhausted days, that idea hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel like myself again, not… that.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels fleeting, the spark of enjoyment is gone, and most days carry a dull, heavy sadness. Nights bring racing worries about your infant's safety and sudden waves of panic, leaving you drained and struggling to sleep even when your little one finally settles. You described moving through feedings, laundry, and texts "on autopilot," feeling like you're "wading through wet sand" and fearing tears you hold back because "once I start I won't be able to stop."
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports she can still laugh but only briefly and without the previous light feeling, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory joy, describing actions as obligation-driven with no emotional spark.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("brain jumps to..."), matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes ('sudden wave…chest tight…shaky') that occur repeatedly ('a couple of times') and cause lingering distress, aligning with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelming stress and impaired coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes racing thoughts and lying awake until 2 a.m. on multiple nights, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, near-daily low mood with near-tears and pervasive grayness, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent near-crying episodes and emotional suppression, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 21 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your daily low mood, near-total loss of interest, nightly ruminative worries, and repeated panic-like symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for a moderate to severe episode. The combination of depressive and anxious features is common in the postpartum period and warrants prompt clinical attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss medication and therapy options
2. Ask about starting evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> designed for postpartum women
3. Plan brief daily walks and 5-minute breathing or mindfulness exercises to gently reduce <sym>anxiety</sym> and improve <sym>sleep</sym>
4. Share these screening results with a trusted support person so they can help coordinate appointments and assist with night-time infant care when possible
5. Continue monitoring your mood and safety; call 988 or local emergency services immediately if thoughts of self-harm ever arise
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Demographic: Postpartum mother, infant present.

Responses obtained via EPDS‐style inquiry.

Affect & Mood  
- Endorsed persistent low mood (“gray filter”), anhedonia, diminished ability to enjoy previously pleasurable activities.  
- Multiple days per week of near-tearfulness; suppresses crying from fear of “not being able to stop.”  
- Describes “heavy blanket” of being overwhelmed by routine infant-care tasks.

Anxiety Spectrum  
- Nocturnal hyper-vigilance regarding infant safety (re-checks breathing x3–4); associated racing heart and difficulty returning to sleep.  
- Sudden episodes of chest tightness/shakiness interpreted as impending doom (consistent with spontaneous panic).  
- Generalized worry “for no good reason,” worst at night.

Cognitive / Self-appraisal  
- Self-blame when infant fussy (“must be something I did”).  
- Racing thoughts reviewing “everything I did wrong,” contributing to initial insomnia.

Functional Impact  
- Daily tasks completed “on autopilot,” described as “wading through wet sand”; evenings marked by emotional exhaustion.

Sleep  
- Initial insomnia linked to ruminative worry; multiple nights/week, 2 a.m. still awake after infant settled.

Safety  
- Denied any thoughts of self-harm; no suicidal ideation voiced.

Summary of Screening Significance  
Endorsed symptoms consistent with probable postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety: persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, excessive guilt, prominent nocturnal anxiety/panic, and related sleep disruption. No self-harm ideation. Recommend formal clinical interview and standardized rating scales (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7) to determine severity and guide next-level care.
